chapter: Starting out in New York and Chicago
title: Chicago band members: Omar Simeon and Walter Fuller
summary: Horace picks out Omar Simeon, a sight-reading first alto who once subbed in Fletcher's band, and trumpeter Walter Fuller who 'sold' a number like Basin Street.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: This particular picture we're looking at here now -- here's a guy you've got to know because he was one of the greats of jazz on the clarinet. He played a lot
of Dixieland later on -- Omar Simeon.

That was my first alto saxophonist. He was originally with Earl Hines, but he was an excellent musician. Oh, he could -- he was a great first man. In fact, he led that section. And when I say sight readers for the benefit of the young kids that don't know about that -- we'd be playing in the first or second bar, and his eyes were on the fourth and fifth. He came in Fletcher's band one night when Fletcher's first alto player was ill, and read Fletcher's book at sight without a rehearsal or anything, didn't miss anything even with the reed choruses -- in those days -- those special choruses where the saxophone's (Singing). He read that right down, and the guys looked at each other. He was great.

And also in my band there's another great guy -- I've got two here that you might know. You remember a great trumpet player that sounds like Louis and they said he played like him which nobody has ever, but he was imitating Louis. Walter Fuller.
Oh yes. That name's well known.

He is living in San Diego. He got -- he moved to San Diego. I'm talking crazy right now. But he got his own group down there. He stayed on the job for 20 years. The last I heard of him, he was still on the job and
Oh I see, in the same job down there.

Same job in San Diego, cause Walter Fuller was a great trumpet player and a salesman. He was in Earl Hines' band when Earl went to New York and broke it up at the Apollo Theater, and his favorite tune that he did was "Rosetta." Do you remember Earl Hines made a record of that, "Rosetta," and of course Walter Fuller had a little baby girl and he named her "Rosetta." And of course, he sang it and played and he was a great musician.
What do you mean when you say salesman? He would --

Selling. With his horn in front of the band being featured. You know, he knew how to put a number over. I'm glad you mentioned this. He could sing "Basin Street," and come out in front of the band, and you would picture yourself as being in New Orleans when he got through. This is what I meant by selling.
